title: Ruby2Shell and Six More Ruby Flaws (CVE-2026-132825): What We Know & What to Do
summary: Seven memory corruption flaws in Ruby's regular expression engine and string case conversion were fixed on November 18, 2026, including Ruby2Shell (CVE-2026-132825). Here is what is public so far, who is exposed and how to get protected before you patch.
body_markdown:
###### TL;DR


##### ‍
***The Ruby core team has fixed seven memory corruption vulnerabilities in Ruby's regular expression engine and in the way Ruby changes the case of strings. Ruby's maintainers say proofs of concept show that some of them can lead to remote code execution. This page tracks what is public, explains what it means for the Ruby applications you run and shows how Miggo can protect you while you upgrade.***


***Last updated:*** November 19, 2026, 10:49 IST. This page is updated on a rolling basis as new details become public.


## **The Short of It**


- On November 18, 2026, the Ruby core team disclosed seven vulnerabilities in Ruby's regular expression engine and string case conversion, and released Ruby 4.0.10, 3.4.13 and 3.3.14 to fix them.
- Most of the flaws do not have CVE identifiers yet. The first to receive one is[CVE-2026-132825](https://www.miggo.io/vulnerability-database/cve/CVE-2026-132825) , a one-byte heap overflow in string case conversion that researchers at Veria Labs have named Ruby2Shell.
- Ruby's maintainers say they are aware of proofs of concept showing that some of these flaws can be used for remote code execution. Even where code execution is not reached, **a crafted request can crash the Ruby process** and take the application down with it.
- Miggo has reproduced a DoS on Rails and Sinatra applications.
- Ruby 3.2 and earlier have reached end of life and will not receive these fixes.
- Miggo customers can mitigate before patching using a Miggo WAF rule, available ahead of the market, that blocks the main primitive responsible for RCE.
- AWS WAF customers can get immediate protection by subscribing to Miggo's Partner Managed Rulesets natively through the AWS WAF console or by subscribing[here](https://aws.amazon.com/marketplace/pp/prodview-6zieu7lxn5vje) .
- Miggo customers are also receiving mitigation and remediation instructions on how else to protect themselves until they can patch.
- No exploitation in the wild has been reported as of publication.


## **What Are the Ruby Regexp and String Vulnerabilities?**


Ruby is the language behind Ruby on Rails and behind widely deployed products such as GitLab, GitHub Enterprise Server, Mastodon and Discourse. The seven flaws sit in two parts of Ruby itself, which means every application running an affected Ruby version carries them, whatever gems it uses.


**The first group is in string case conversion.** When Ruby changes the case of text with methods such as upcase, swapcase, downcase(:fold) or casecmp?, it can write past the end of the memory buffer it allocated. Ruby2Shell is the clearest example. In many single-byte encodings, such as ISO-8859-1 and Windows-1252, the German letter ß has no single-character uppercase form, so Ruby writes two characters where it checked room for one. An attacker only needs to send text that the application changes the case of, a regular operation in Ruby on Rails and similar applications.


**The second group is in the regular expression engine.** Four of these flaws are triggered when an application compiles, matches or prints a regular expression pattern that an attacker supplied, which matters for applications that build patterns from user input, such as search and filtering features. The fifth is triggered by the text being matched rather than the pattern, and can disclose memory contents or crash the process.


Separately these vulnerabilities may be low-impact, but chained together they can form a more potent vulnerability.

## **Which of Your Applications Are Actually Exposed?**


Knowing that you run Ruby is not enough to plan a response. Three questions decide whether a given application is at risk: whether the running process uses an affected Ruby version, whether attackers can reach it, and whether attacker input actually reaches the vulnerable code. For the case conversion flaws, that means request text being upcased, downcased or compared without regard to case. For four of the regular expression flaws, it means a pattern built from user input.


Miggo answers those questions from runtime evidence. Using DeepTracing™, Miggo maps the Ruby applications that are actually running in your environment, the Ruby versions they run on and how they are exposed to the internet. Because of where these vulnerabilities live, Miggo’s profiling is used to determine exploitability and whether affected functions are running. That lets your team start the rollout with the internet-facing applications that matter most, instead of working through an inventory of every Ruby installation.


## **How Miggo Protects You Before the Patch**


Miggo Mitigation Lab analyzed all seven Ruby flaws and built a WAF rule that blocks the main primitive responsible for remote code execution, the one-byte heap write in string case conversion behind Ruby2Shell. Miggo customers have this protection ahead of the market, and it can be in place within minutes, without code changes and without waiting for every application to be rebuilt on a fixed Ruby.


At the edge, Miggo generates WAF rules that run in the web application firewall you already use. AWS WAF customers can get immediate protection by subscribing to Miggo’s Partner Managed Rulesets natively through the AWS WAF console or by subscribing[here](https://aws.amazon.com/marketplace/pp/prodview-6zieu7lxn5vje) . The rule will be continuously updated as more information and new exploits emerge, so subscribed customers will receive updated versions for continuous mitigation.


## **What to Do Now**


1. Find every Ruby runtime in your environment, including application servers, background workers, container base images, distribution packages and products that bundle their own Ruby, such as GitLab and GitHub Enterprise Server.
2. Upgrade to Ruby 4.0.10, 3.4.13 or 3.3.14, rebuild the images that depend on it and install your vendors' fixed releases as soon as they are available.
3. Restart your application processes and verify the Ruby version that the running process reports, not only the version that is installed.
4. If you run Ruby 3.2 or earlier, plan the migration to a supported version and put a runtime mitigation in place until it is complete.
5. Put a mitigation, such as a WAF rule, in front of the applications you cannot patch right away.
6. Review code that builds regular expressions from user input.
7. Watch for unexpected crashes and restarts of Ruby worker processes such as Puma, Unicorn and Sidekiq, and for requests that declare legacy character encodings such as ISO-8859-1 or Windows-1252.


## **Get Protected While You Patch**


Miggo can show you which of your Ruby applications are exposed to Ruby2Shell and the other six Ruby flaws, and protect them while your team rolls out the fix.


If you’re concerned about these Ruby vulnerabilities, our team can help you find exposed applications and put protection in place right away.[Contact us here](https://www.miggo.io/book-a-demo)
